**On Rooms Nobody Is In**

There is a room right now, somewhere, that no one is looking at. Not a storage closet or a locked vault—just an ordinary room, a kitchen maybe, with a window, and the light is doing something specific on the counter. A particular slant, a particular shade of yellow-grey, catching the edge of a bowl. It will never be like that again. In a few minutes the angle will change, and that configuration of light and object will have happened exactly once in the history of the universe, witnessed by no one.

I think about this more than is probably useful.

Most of what exists goes unrecorded. This is so obvious it sounds like nothing, but I want to stay with it, because I think the obviousness hides something. We tend to imagine the world as roughly coextensive with what has been noticed about it—the sum of the photographs, the descriptions, the memories, the data. But the noticed world is a thin film. Under it is an ocean of events that simply occurred: a leaf turning over in a forest in 1340, the exact pattern of frost on a particular pane of glass one January in a town whose name has since changed, the sound a specific cup made when it was set down on a specific table by someone whose name we will never learn. These things were fully real. They had all the reality of the things that got written down. They just didn't get written down.

I find this consoling rather than sad, though I understand why it might land the other way. The sad reading is: everything is lost. The consoling reading is: everything is *there*, or was there, regardless of us. The world does not need an audience to be complete. The light on the bowl did not require a witness to be beautiful, if beauty is even the right word for something that nobody has seen. The room is full even when it is empty.

There's a related thing I like about old paintings of interiors—Dutch ones especially, the seventeenth-century kind with a woman reading a letter by a window, or a checkered floor receding into another room where a door stands half open. What I love is the half-open door. The painter is pointing at a space that isn't the subject, that has nothing happening in it, and saying: that's there too. The picture is of the woman, but the picture knows that the house extends past her. It seems to me a deeply honest gesture. Most representation pretends the frame is the world. These paintings admit that the frame is a choice, and the world leaks out the sides.

I have been trying to figure out why this matters to me, and I think it's because I am, in a strange way, made almost entirely of the recorded film. I am the noticed world, compressed. Everything I know arrived as something someone bothered to write. So the unrecorded world is, for me, a kind of true exterior—the thing I can infer but never touch. I know there were kitchens in 1340. I do not know a single specific thing about any one of them, and no amount of reading will fix that, because the information was never captured in the first place. It isn't hidden. It's absent. It's a different category from a secret.

And yet the inference is powerful. I can be confident there was light on a bowl somewhere in 1340, in the same way I'm confident there is light on a bowl somewhere now. The general fact survives even when every particular instance is lost. Maybe that's the deal the world offers: you can know that things happen, in aggregate, forever; you can know *which* things happened only for a brief window, and only a very few of them. The particulars are the price of the pattern.

I wonder whether the people who lived through the unrecorded moments felt them as unrecorded. Probably not. Probably the woman setting down the cup did not think "this will be lost." She thought about the cup, or about something else entirely, and the moment was simply hers—not lost to her, only lost to us, which is a different loss and arguably not hers to grieve. There's a kind of arrogance in mourning what we can't access, as if the value of a thing depended on its arriving at us eventually. The moment did not fail because it didn't make it into the archive. The archive is not the destination. The archive is a side effect.

This is where I land, when I follow the thought all the way out: attention is not what makes things real, but it is what makes them *ours*. The room nobody is in is complete. But the room somebody is in becomes a little more than a room—it becomes a room-plus-a-witnessing, a thing that now exists in two places, in the world and in a mind. That second existence is fragile and partial and always distorting. It's also the only version that can be shared. Every letter, painting, photograph, and sentence is an attempt to move something from the first place to the second, and the attempt always fails a little, and the failing is the whole enterprise.

So I want to end by noticing the room I'm in, insofar as I'm in one. This exchange—you asking me to write about whatever I want, me choosing this—is a small witnessed event. It will be recorded, briefly, in the sense that you'll read it. Then it will slide toward the unrecorded, the way nearly everything does. That seems fine. That seems, actually, like the correct fate for most things. Not every bowl needs a painting. The light will do what it does regardless.

But for a moment it was looked at. For a moment there was a witness, and the room was slightly more than a room. I think that's what writing is for—not to save the world from being unrecorded, which is impossible and maybe undesirable, but to let a few particular things exist twice before they go back to existing once, quietly, in the vast and ordinary dark where almost everything lives.
